target: spread_bps at the scored day, as the 23-quantile distribution at each lead h = 1..5 (scoring_protocol.GRID)
why: protocol_benchmarks.b1_forecast adds the trailing two years' h-row changes to the last public spread. The last public row (the anchor) is older than the decision day: for the decision on row t the anchor is row t - L, where L is the lag in business rows (1 on an ordinary day). The elapsed horizon from the anchor to the target row t + h is therefore h + L, which a mean-reverting candidate uses and B1 does not. The outside review calls this a design mismatch to test, not proof that a corrected B1 scores better. This study measures it.
decision_instant: 18:00 America/New_York (docs/decisions/information-set.md as amended by #1312; every command sets RMM_DECISION_TIME=18:00). The anchor is the one the 18:00 InformationRule gives
lag: L = decision_index - anchor, in rows of the published panel (business days), the same for every lead of one decision day (protocol_benchmarks._anchor requires the leads to agree). The horizon of the change is H = h + L. The study reports the distribution of L over the scored decision days

arms.B1: protocol_benchmarks.b1_forecast, unchanged: the anchor's spread plus the empirical quantiles of spread[s] - spread[s - h] for s in range(max(first, h), anchor + 1)

B1_star.label: B1*
B1_star.definition: identical to B1 except that the change window is anchor-to-target: the changes are spread[s] - spread[s - H], H = h + L, for s in range(max(first, H), anchor + 1), where first is B1's window start (the first row after the decision day less two years). The centre is the anchor's spread, as in B1

arms.B1_prime: repo_model.b1_calendar.b1_calendar_forecast (#960, metadata/b1_calendar_960.json), unchanged: the anchor is the last ordinary spread at or before the anchor; the changes spread[e] - last_ordinary[e - h] for e in range(max(first, h), anchor + 1) with an ordinary row at or before e - h; pooled by the reporting day type of the target day, a pool of fewer than 30 changes falling back to every type

B1_prime_star.label: B1'*
B1_prime_star.definition: identical to B1' except that the change window is anchor-to-target: the changes are spread[e] - last_ordinary[e - H], H = h + L, for e in range(max(first, H), anchor + 1) with an ordinary row at or before e - H. The centre (the last ordinary spread at or before the anchor), the pool by the target day's reporting day type and the floor of 30 are B1''s

arms.candidate: sc_s3c_ann_net, (s3c-ann-net) of docs/research/h5-candidate.json, walked with the code of scripts/s3c_announced_settlement_1288.py unchanged (its build) at the 18:00 instant. No candidate change

reads: every row B1* and B1'* read is at or before the anchor; protocol_benchmarks._require_public restates it for the rows read, on the starting rows as well as the ending rows (LookAheadError otherwise). No parameter is fitted

windows.development: decision days whose five targets fall on or before 2025-12-31 (the frame of #1255, as scripts/s3c_announced_settlement_1288.py builds it)
windows.2026: decision days whose five targets fall from 2026-01-02 to 2026-09-03 (the 2026 development days of #1229, the near-blind tier open since GO #151). Development data on seen days; it decides nothing

metrics.grid_crps: grid CRPS (23 levels) averaged over leads h = 1..5, the primary score
metrics.upper_tail_twcrps: upper-tail twCRPS (weight 1{z > 0 bp}), the key secondary
metrics.brier_gt5: the Brier score of P(spread > +5 bp), the probability read off the 23 quantiles as in docs/decisions/pressure-probability.md, the event strict and on whole basis points

pairs.reading: for a pair (a, b), a is the arm and b the reference; skill above zero favours a. The correction pairs say whether the anchor-to-target window scores better than the original on its own

split_note: pooled, by lead h = 1..5, by regime (the development window; the 2026 days are one regime), by pressure-day type (turn_days labels of the target day) and by the calendar day type of the target. A group of fewer than 20 days is listed, not tested (MIN_GROUP_DAYS). The month split of the family is not run: it answers a different question
absolute_losses: for every model and every group the study reports the mean of each metric next to the skill ratios, so a ratio is never the only figure; and the mean-d bound (the studentized stationary bootstrap interval on the mean paired loss difference d = S(reference) - S(arm), her ruling on #1009) for every tested pair

scoring.scorer: repo_model.scoring_protocol (#655), the development tier: no verdict, no registration
scoring.test: scoring_protocol.paired_tests, the studentized stationary bootstrap, mean block 10 business days, 10,000 draws, seed 1388, two-sided 90% interval (the lower end is the one-sided 95% bound); the skill interval and the interval on mean d are reported for every tested row
scoring.reading: a gain is read when the lower end of the 90% interval of mean d is above zero, a loss when its upper end is below zero, otherwise undecided (her ruling on #1009). A point estimate alone is not read

reading_rules: A figure is a check on days that were already seen. Nothing here is a verdict, nothing is registered and no choice is made on it.
A pooled figure is never read without the lead, regime and day-type splits beside it.
The review's claim is a design mismatch to test: a corrected B1 that scores no better than B1 is a result, not a failure of the study.

A benchmark that scores worse in absolute loss is a weaker reference, so the candidate's skill against it is larger; the page says so wherever a skill ratio against a corrected benchmark falls or rises.

The page ends with a marked question for Eleonora with numbered options and a default: whether B1* and B1'* replace B1 and B1' in the registered comparison. Recommendation and default: B1'* is the mandatory persistence benchmark, legacy B1 reported for continuity.
